questions.question: What is the 'Common Trap: Wrong Direction'?
options: Choosing an option that reverses the relationship's original direction
A trap unrelated to relationship direction
A trap only in number analogies
A trap that never actually occurs
questions.rationale: This trap, related to the earlier Direction Trap, involves choosing an option that has the right general relationship but applies it in the reversed direction.

questions.question: What is the 'Common Trap: Multiple Relations'?
options: A pair with no relationship at all
A trap that only applies to a single relationship type
A situation where an item pair has more than one plausible relationship, making the intended one ambiguous without careful analysis
A trap unrelated to analogy solving
questions.rationale: This trap arises when a given pair could plausibly be connected by more than one relationship, requiring careful analysis to determine which one the question actually intends.

questions.question: What does a 'Speed Strategy for Exams' balance, in analogy reasoning?
options: Only accuracy, ignoring speed entirely
Quickly recognizing common relationship patterns while still verifying against the golden rule before finalizing an answer
Only speed, with no verification
Randomly guessing to save time
questions.rationale: A good speed strategy balances quick pattern recognition with still properly verifying the relationship against the golden rule before committing to a final answer.

questions.question: What might a '10-Second Mental Checklist' include?
options: A lengthy, multi-step derivation
A checklist with no practical use
Only number-based checks
A short list of the most common relationship categories to quickly check against a given pair
questions.rationale: This checklist provides a short, fast-to-run-through list of the most common relationship categories, helping quickly narrow down which type applies.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of 'Solved Examples 1 through 11' in this part of the lesson?
options: To demonstrate the solving process applied to a range of realistic analogy problems, reinforcing the techniques already covered
To introduce entirely new relationship types
To replace the need for the golden rule
To only test letter analogies
questions.rationale: These worked examples demonstrate the solving process on a range of realistic problems, reinforcing the techniques and relationship types already introduced earlier in the lesson.

questions.question: Why does a lesson typically include MANY solved examples (11 or more) rather than just one or two?
options: Extra examples have no additional value
Because a single example is always sufficient
Repeated exposure across varied examples helps reinforce pattern recognition across different relationship types
Because later examples repeat the exact same relationship
questions.rationale: Working through many varied examples helps reinforce pattern recognition across the different relationship types, building the fluency needed to recognize them quickly.

questions.question: What should you do if a solved example's answer doesn't match your own derivation?
options: Assume you are always right and move on
Re-examine your stated relationship and verification against the golden rule to find the discrepancy
Ignore the solved example entirely
Assume the example is always wrong
questions.rationale: A mismatch signals a need to re-examine your own stated relationship and verification, since the systematic method (golden rule, full verification) is what should reliably produce the correct answer.

questions.question: Why is working through solved examples covering DIFFERENT relationship types (geography, science, numbers, letters) valuable?
options: It has no added value over repeating one type
It only helps with number analogies
Only one relationship type actually appears in exams
It builds broad familiarity across the full range of relationship categories likely to appear in real questions
questions.rationale: Since real exam questions can draw from any of the many relationship categories covered, practicing across a diverse range builds the broad familiarity needed to recognize whichever type appears.

questions.question: What connects a 'Speed Strategy' with the earlier 'Principle of Simplest Rule'?
options: They are unrelated concepts
Both aim to make solving faster and more reliable by preferring straightforward, well-verified approaches over complex guesswork
Speed strategy replaces the need for any rule identification
The principle of simplest rule only applies to numbers
questions.rationale: Both concepts share the goal of efficient, reliable solving — preferring straightforward, verifiable approaches (simplest rule, quick pattern checks) over complex, unverified guesswork.

questions.question: Why is a '10-Second Mental Checklist' only useful AFTER the underlying relationship categories have already been learned?
options: It isn't actually dependent on prior learning
A quick checklist only works as a fast recall aid once you already know what each category means from deeper study
The checklist teaches the categories from scratch
Order of learning never matters
questions.rationale: A fast checklist is a recall aid, not a teaching tool — it only works efficiently once the underlying relationship categories have already been properly learned through deeper study.
